deep.reconstruction:
Context: Euler, Tractatus de numerorum doctrina, Cap. 7. §§203–211 on the previous page used a coset-type argument. The residues 1, b, b^2, ..., b^(n-1) mod d form a set closed under multiplication. The remaining units ('non-residua') split into blocks x·{residues} of size n. Hence phi(d) = k·n for some integer k. On this page Euler draws the consequences.

§212: Let gcd(b,d)=1 and mu = phi(d), the number of integers below d coprime to d. Let n be the least positive exponent with b^n ≡ 1 (mod d), i.e. n = ord_d(b). Then n = mu/m for some divisor m of mu. So the order divides phi(d), as shown in §§207–211.

§213: Since b^n ≡ 1, also b^(kn) ≡ 1 for every k. Taking k = m gives b^(mn) = b^mu ≡ 1 (mod d). Hence d | b^phi(d) - 1 whenever gcd(b,d)=1. This is Euler's theorem.

§214: If also gcd(c,d)=1, then d | c^mu - 1. Subtracting, d | b^mu - c^mu.

§215: For d = p prime, mu = p-1, so p | b^(p-1) - 1 unless p | b. This is Fermat's little theorem. A smaller exponent n with p | b^n - 1 may occur, but then n must divide p-1.

§216: For d = pq with p ≠ q primes and b divisible by neither, mu = (p-1)(q-1). Hence pq | b^((p-1)(q-1)) - 1.

§217: For d = p^lambda q^mu r^nu s^xi with distinct primes, put m = p^(lambda-1)(p-1) q^(mu-1)(q-1) r^(nu-1)(r-1) s^(xi-1)(s-1). This is the multiplicative formula for phi(d), which Euler uses without proof here (it was presumably established earlier in the treatise). Then d | b^m - 1 for b coprime to d. Sometimes b^n - 1 with n a proper divisor of m is already divisible.

§218: Return to general d, with mu = phi(d) and n = ord_d(b). Necessarily n ∈ {mu, mu/2, mu/3, mu/4, mu/5, ...}, as far as these are integers. Euler announces a closer study of these cases.

§219: Conjecture/programme: which divisor occurs depends on b. Some b give n = mu (in modern terms, primitive roots), others mu/2, mu/3, etc.

§220: For any divisor n of mu, if b^n ≡ 1 and c^n ≡ 1, then (bc)^n = b^n c^n ≡ 1. Also (b ± lambda d)^n ≡ b^n ≡ 1 (mod d), by the binomial theorem (my filling). So the property depends only on b mod d, and the solutions of x^n ≡ 1 form a multiplicatively closed set.

§221: Since b^mu ≡ 1 always, Euler next asks for which b one also has b^(mu/2) ≡ 1. This requires mu to be even, which holds for all d except d = 2 (and trivially d = 1). The next page answers this with squares: b = e^2 gives b^(mu/2) = e^mu ≡ 1.
errors: No mathematical errors on this page.

§217 notational clash: the exponent mu of q in d = p^lambda q^mu r^nu s^xi reuses the symbol mu, which elsewhere denotes phi(d). Similarly, m in §217 means phi(d), whereas in §212 m means the cofactor mu/n.
§217 uses the product formula phi(p^a q^b ...) = prod p^(a-1)(p-1) without justification on this page; it is presumably proved earlier in the treatise.
§221 'mu is even unless d = 2' tacitly excludes d = 1 (phi(1) = 1). This is harmless.
§212/§218: 'pars aliquota' must be read as including mu itself (m = 1), as Euler indicates with 'vel n = mu'.

results.what: The multiplicative order of b mod d divides phi(d) (via the coset-partition argument of §§207–211)
results.modern_name: Lagrange's theorem for the unit group (Z/dZ)^*; order of an element divides the group order
results.usually_credited_to: Euler (E262, E271, c. 1758–1763); general group form Lagrange/Cauchy/Jordan
Euler, 1763 (E271, Theoremata arithmetica nova methodo demonstrata)

results.what: p | b^(p-1) - 1 for a prime p not dividing b; any n with p | b^n - 1 minimal divides p-1
results.modern_name: Fermat's little theorem; order divides p-1
results.usually_credited_to: Fermat (1640, statement), Euler (first published proofs 1736/1741, E54, E134, E262)

results.modern_name: Product formula for Euler's totient function

results.what: Solutions of b^n ≡ 1 (mod d) are closed under multiplication and depend only on b mod d
results.modern_name: Kernel of the n-th power map is a subgroup of (Z/dZ)^*

results.modern_name: Primitive roots and power residues; Euler's criterion setup

deep.surprise_reason: This is the well-known Tractatus de numerorum doctrina (Opera posthuma 1849). It contains Euler's own theorem b^phi(d) ≡ 1 with his published coset proof, and the totient product formula. All of this is standard and firmly credited to Euler.

checkable.sympy: all((pow(b, totient(d), d) == 1) for d in range(2, 200) for b in range(1, d) if gcd(b, d) == 1)
checkable.asserts: Euler's theorem: d | b^phi(d) - 1 for gcd(b,d) = 1 (§213)

checkable.sympy: all(totient(d) % n_order(b, d) == 0 for d in range(2, 200) for b in range(1, d) if gcd(b, d) == 1)
checkable.asserts: The order n of b mod d divides mu = phi(d) (§212)

checkable.sympy: all((pow(b, p-1, p) == 1) for p in primerange(2, 200) for b in range(1, p))
all(totient(p*q) == (p-1)*(q-1) for p in primerange(2, 50) for q in primerange(2, 50) if p != q)

checkable.asserts: Totient product formula of §217 for a four-prime example

checkable.sympy: all(pow((b*c) % d, n, d) == 1 for d in range(2, 60) for n in divisors(totient(d)) for b in range(1, d) for c in range(1, d) if gcd(b*c, d) == 1 and pow(b, n, d) == 1 and pow(c, n, d) == 1)
checkable.asserts: §220: if b^n ≡ 1 and c^n ≡ 1 then (bc)^n ≡ 1 mod d
§221: mu = phi(d) is even for all d > 2
